title.narrative: The Green Evolution: Pathways to Transforming Food Systems in India, Bangladesh and Nepal

description.narrative: Overall objective: To contribute to robust local food systems in India, Nepal, and Bangladesh that safeguard people’s right to safe healthy food, promote food sovereignty for local communities and build up resilience to climate change (SDG2)Project Goal: Stakeholders, particularly farmers and local authorities, transition to ecological food production systems through improved policy frameworks, convergence with (and within) government programmes, and civil society cooperation at national, regional and global levels

The exact numbers of direct target groups will be arrived at during the baseline. However, indicative figures are as follows:(1) Approximately 16.000 smallholder farmer households with one farmer from each household (40% women) which will be clustered into 600 Groups; (2) 11000 additional farmers reached out through climate information service; (3) 4200 Community members reached out through food system dialogues and food system analysis (50% Women); (4) 50 food entrepreneurs (micro level)500 elected representatives and bureaucrats at various level of the governments; (5) 3000 extension workers from relevant departments of state and national government; (6) 510 students (50% women) and 135 civil society members (40% women) as influencers reached out through capacity building.Altogether, the project will reach out to approximately 35345 individuals directly (13355 in India, 11695 in Bangladesh and 10295 in Nepal). Institutional direct target groups: (1) 15 community institutions (Producer Groups, Resource Users Groups associated with landscape management or common facility centers for processing); (2) local governments at village and watershed level (micro level); (3) District/province governments (meso level); (4) 6 Academic/ research institutions/Universities (meso level); (5) 6 national level and 3 international networks for policy advocacy (macro level).Indirect target groups: (1) 768,300 farmer family members will be indirectly benefited from the landscape level initiatives, services provided by common facility centers and capacity building provided by the extension workers trained by the proposed project. (2) 506,000 urban/semiurban consumers who benefit from the campaign and newly offered products from the food ecopreneurs in the nodal towns, semi-urban and urban areas in the targeted districts.Altogether, the project is expected to reach out to 1.274.300 individuals indirectly (574500 in India, 449900 in Bangladesh, 249900 in Nepal)

Today's food systems are designed to produce/market/consume cheap, starchy calories for a growing world population. However, the concerns of the 21st century are the intersections of chronic diseases, improved but continuing food insecurity, undernutrition, and sustainability. This requires a fundamental transformation of food systems to meet evolving and future needs of consumers, producers, and the resource base on which all life depends. Agroecological principles are increasingly seen as being able, or even necessary, to achieve such transformation of food systems (HLPE 2019) and increase resilience to climatic shocks. However, there are various barriers to an agroecological transition at scale at the micro (Farm and watershed scale), meso (District and regional scale) and macro (State, National and Global scale).
